Chapter 3: Life Under Constant Threat and the Erosion of Identity
When someone else controls every part of your life, it changes the way you see the world—and yourself. For this girl, each and every day felt like a test. She was just trying to hold on to the smallest pieces of who she used to be.
The man who held her captive decided everything. There was no such thing as privacy. She didn’t even get to have her own thoughts—he was always there, setting the rules, and these rules seemed to change all the time. One day, something might be okay. The next, it could get her into trouble. She learned pretty quickly to move quietly, to study his moods, and to do whatever she could to avoid being noticed. But the fear of messing up? It was always there, buzzing quietly in the back of her mind.
And it wasn’t just about physical pain. He used words like weapons, chipping away at her confidence, convincing her that she was unlovable, not smart enough, and weak. He told her nobody else would ever want her, that she should be grateful he was there—even as he hurt her. It’s hard to imagine, but after a while, she started to believe him. The line between truth and his manipulations got so blurry that she didn’t trust her own thoughts anymore.
Isolation was her new normal. She was cut off from her family, her friends, and everything happening outside those walls. Sometimes she’d hear voices or footsteps, but she knew better than to call out for help. He’d warned her that nobody would believe her, that everything was her fault. The shame and fear kept her quiet.
Every now and then, she’d try to remember who she was before all this happened. The girl who loved to read, who dreamed about traveling, who used to laugh with friends. But those memories felt so far away—like flashes from someone else’s life. She couldn’t help but wonder: could she ever get back to that person, or was she lost for good?
Still, even in the darkest moments, she found small ways to survive. She’d count the days, mark time in her mind, and create tiny routines that gave her a sense of control. She’d look for comfort in little things—a patch of sunlight, the sound of rain against the window, the gentle rhythm of her own breathing. Those moments reminded her that she was still here, still able to feel something besides fear.
It’s easy to underestimate just how quickly a person’s sense of self can fade away under constant abuse. It isn’t just the pain or the loneliness—it’s the slow, steady drain of hope.
But even as her world shrank down to just a single room, she never completely let go of the idea that things could change. She didn’t know how, or when, but she kept holding on to the hope that one day, she might be free.
